 ATP Finals Carlos Alcaraz flies past Flavio Cobolli in ATP Finals tennis group stage – as it happened
 Alcaraz appeared untroubled by his hamstring injury as he made it three straight-sets wins from three with a 6-4, 6-1 demolition of the Italian
  Updated  29m ago Katy Murrells Fri 20 Nov 2026 10.05 EST First published on Fri 20 Nov 2026 07.01 EST Share Key events 37m ago Alcaraz maintains perfect record despite hamstring injury 
 1h ago Alcaraz defeats Cobolli 6-4, 6-1 
 2h ago Alcaraz wins the first set 6-4 
 4h ago Preamble 
 Carlos Alcaraz stoops to make a forehand return to Flavio Cobolli. Photograph: Marco Bertorello/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Carlos Alcaraz stoops to make a forehand return to Flavio Cobolli. Photograph: Marco Bertorello/AFP/Getty Images Katy Murrells Fri 20 Nov 2026 10.05 EST First published on Fri 20 Nov 2026 07.01 EST Share Key events 37m ago Alcaraz maintains perfect record despite hamstring injury 
 1h ago Alcaraz defeats Cobolli 6-4, 6-1 
 2h ago Alcaraz wins the first set 6-4 
 4h ago Preamble 
 28m ago 10.05 EST Thanks for your company today – we’ll be back with semi-final coverage tomorrow. Ciao !
 Share 37m ago 09.57 EST Alcaraz maintains perfect record despite hamstring injury
 Carlos Alcaraz did not appear bothered by his various physical issues in a 6-4, 6-1 victory over home player Flavio Cobolli at the ATP Finals on Friday.
 The seven-time grand slam champion broke his Italian opponent’s serve in the opening game of both sets and ended points quickly. Alcaraz finished the match off in 65 minutes and had a huge advantage of 29-9 in winners.
 “I tried to play as aggressive as I can — hitting the ball as hard as I could, trying not to move that much,” Alcaraz said.
 Alcaraz had strapping on his injured left hamstring and a strip of tape on his right knee. Alcaraz hurt his hamstring in his previous match against Daniil Medvedev. He also missed four and a half months this year because of a right wrist injury.
 “The challenge now is not on the court but off the court,” Alcaraz said, “to do whatever it takes to be in a good shape, to feel physically ready for tomorrow. It’s going to be a really important half a day that I have ahead of me with my team, with my physio, with the doctor.”
 Alcaraz had already secured a place in the semi-finals against Ben Shelton at the season-ending event and completed group play with a perfect three wins. The semi-final will be a rematch of the US Open quarter-final between Shelton and Alcaraz that ended at 3.33am.
 While Shelton won that five-set clash in New York, Alcaraz recently got revenge in the Paris Masters final.
 In the other semi-final, top-ranked Alexander Zverev will face Medvedev or Frances Tiafoe, who play later on Friday. Cobolli’s Turin debut ended with three losses.
 Alcaraz is attempting to win the ATP Finals title for the first time, having lost to Jannik Sinner in the final a year ago.
 Alcaraz extended his winning streak to 12 matches after titles in Vienna and Paris. “The way I felt on the court today was incredible,” Alcaraz said. “I’m getting more confident after every match.” Associated Press 
 Share Updated at  10.02 EST 47m ago 09.46 EST Share 1h ago 09.37 EST I think he probably felt the hamstring a little – he certainly wasn’t as smiley and engaged with the crowd as he usually is – but he did such a good job of dictating the match and keeping the points short, that he’s given himself the best possible chance of being ready for Shelton tomorrow … and then perhaps Zverev in the final. I don’t think he’d take any unnecessary risks, if the injury was serious playing on wouldn’t be worth the gamble, and at least he knows he can take a break after this tournament (or after the Davis Cup Finals next week if he’s fit enough to take part there).
 Share 1h ago 09.32 EST An email from Christian Miners. “How’s Alcaraz’s mobility looking?” he asks. “I’ve hugely enjoyed his comeback from the last injury – he’s played some dashing musketeer tennis at times –and I’d hate for him to turn a niggle into a serious injury in the run-up to the Aussie Open. I’m also anxious for someone to depose Zverev from his position as ‘#1 by default’ due to the simultaneous absences of the best two men’s players.”
 Share 1h ago 09.30 EST Just one hour and five minutes . Five games conceded. 84% of first-serve points won. 29 winners. Zero break points faced. A dominant display, and he didn’t have to put his hamstring under too much strain. So how’s Alcaraz feeling?
 double quotation mark The challenge now is not on the court but off the court, to be physically ready for the battle tomorrow. It’s going to be really important. I felt great on court today, I tried to be aggressive, dominate as much as I could, to not move too much. I’m proud of my level today.
 Share Updated at  09.43 EST 1h ago 09.22 EST Alcaraz defeats Cobolli 6-4, 6-1
 Alcaraz holds to 15 to make it eight points from the last nine. And 27 winners to Cobolli’s nine. And he doesn’t even need to serve this match out, because the court is shrinking for Cobolli and in the blink of an eye it’s 0-15, 0-30, 0-40 on Cobolli’s serve … and Alcaraz, rather appropriately given the way he’s flattened the Italian’s serve in this second set, secures the victory with a backhand return winner!
 Another Alcaraz masterclass comes to an end. It’s his third consecutive win in straight sets, and for Cobolli his third successive defeat in straight sets. At least the Italian still has the Davis Cup Finals to look forward to next week, while Alcaraz can now focus on being in the best possible shape for his semi-final against Ben Shelton tomorrow. And there’s a nice exchange between the two friends at the net, before Alcaraz applauds Cobolli off court.
 View image in fullscreen Carlos Alcaraz celebrates his straight sets victory. Photograph: Guglielmo Mangiapane/Reuters Share Updated at  09.45 EST 1h ago 09.17 EST Alcaraz breaks: Alcaraz* 6-4, 4-1 Cobolli (*denotes next server) 
 Alcaraz still very much looks all business as he advances to 0-15, 0-30, 0-40. And he absolutely obliterates Cobolli’s serve with a backhand return winner to break to love! After his 6-2, 6-2 win against Tiafoe and 6-2, 6-4 victory over Medvedev, this is just as impressive. Alcaraz usually arrives in Turin tired after a long season but, having had that four-month break in the summer because of his wrist injury, his late-season form has been outstanding. And he’s the man to beat going into the semi-finals.
 Share 1h ago 09.12 EST Second set: Alcaraz 6-4, 3-1 Cobolli* (*denotes next server) 
 At 15-all, Alcaraz hits back behind Cobolli with a dismissive forehand winner. He’s a little lucky on the next point, when one of his forehands clips the tape before going over, but he still wins the rally, and then shows tremendous touch with a little flick to claim the game. There haven’t been as many smiles as usual from Alcaraz today – maybe he just wants to get this over and done with, without any more damage to his hamstring – and he’s got his game face on as the scoreboard ticks over to 6-4, 3-1.
 View image in fullscreen The second set hasn’t been kind to Flavio Cobolli. Photograph: Alessandro Di Marco/EPA Share Updated at  09.22 EST 1h ago 09.08 EST Second set: Alcaraz* 6-4, 2-1 Cobolli (*denotes next server) 
 Cobolli does, at least, ask Alcaraz a few questions on serve in the next game, but Alcaraz comes through to 30, finishing things off with some fireworks at the net. A first love hold for Cobolli follows, but there’s an unconvincing cheer from the crowd. They know this match is Alcaraz’s for the taking.
 Share 2h ago 09.03 EST Alcaraz breaks: Alcaraz* 6-4, 1-0 Cobolli (*denotes next server) 
 Ouch. Just as I’m looking at the first-set stats, Cobolli, off balance on the baseline, clatters his backhand into the net and he’s broken to 30 in the opening game of the second – just as he was at the start of the first. So it’s another headstart for Alcaraz, who’s doing a job on the Italian. The Turin crowd are silenced.
 Share Updated at  09.04 EST 2h ago 08.57 EST Alcaraz wins the first set 6-4
 No, is the short answer. 15-0. 30-0. 40-0. And Alcaraz settles the opener with an unreturned serve out wide. It’s the fifth successive set he’s won this week – and fifth consecutive set that Cobolli has conceded. Tougher tasks will await Alcaraz – with Ben Shelton in the semi-finals tomorrow and then possibly Alexander Zverev in Sunday’s final – but the signs so far are that his left hamstring won’t derail him.
 View image in fullscreen Carlos Alcaraz’s serve helps him take the first set. Photograph: Guglielmo Mangiapane/Reuters Share Updated at  09.18 EST 2h ago 08.54 EST First set: Alcaraz* 5-4 Cobolli (*denotes next server) 
 Ahhahahhaa. Three return winners from Alcaraz and it’s set point at 30-40 . The Turin crowd rhythmically and loudly clap as Cobolli steps up to serve, they’re trying to rouse their man … and they’re soon cheering when Alcaraz is jammed by a body serve. Deuce. Advantage Cobolli. Deuce. Advantage Alcaraz, a second set point , as Cobolli clunks a backhand into the tramlines. Cobolli repels Alcaraz with an unreturned serve. Deuce. Advantage Cobolli. And Cobolli, on the run, sprints left to right with those lightning fast feet to pull off his best shot of the match, a cross-court forehand winner, and even Alcaraz is applauding. He’s saved his best until nearly last in this set, but can he break Alcaraz, who will now serve for the set?
 Share 2h ago 08.47 EST First set: Alcaraz 5-3 Cobolli* (*denotes next server) 
 The net gods are smiling down on Alcaraz when his drop shot clips the tape and trickles over for 15-all, but Cobolli then reminds Alcaraz that his forehand is flashy too, and it’s 15-30. A glimmer for the Italian. Cobolli gets himself into the rally after a second serve … but he inexplicably bashes a backhand into the net. And then looks up to the skies – or more accurately the stadium roof. That was a missed opportunity. And although Alcaraz blinks at 40-30, to give Cobolli deuce for the first time on the Spaniard’s serve, Alcaraz accelerates through the next two points to move within a game of the first set.
 View image in fullscreen Carlos Alcaraz flings a forehand to Flavio Cobolli. Photograph: Guglielmo Mangiapane/Reuters Share Updated at  08.56 EST 2h ago 08.41 EST First set: Alcaraz* 4-3 Cobolli (*denotes next server) 
 Cobolli is feeling the pressure on serve at 30-all. Will it be another break point? Not immediately, because Cobolli calmly hits back behind Alcaraz for the winner, but Alcaraz is the aggressor on the next point and he draws the error from Cobolli for deuce. And then Alcaraz grazes the sideline and baseline with an improbable return winner that defies physics! Break point Alcaraz … but the Spaniard nets a meek backhand. Break point No 2 Alcaraz after a 110mph (!) ninja forehand … but again he nets! And Cobolli somehow survives to limit Alcaraz to just the one break!
 Share Updated at  08.59 EST 2h ago 08.34 EST First set: Alcaraz 4-2 Cobolli* (*denotes next server) 
 On the third point, Alcaraz – stretching and sliding and looking untroubled by that hamstring – finds a vicious angle to combat Cobolli, and it’s 40-0. Cobolli comes back for 40-15 and then 40-30 when Alcaraz nets a volley. So Alcaraz has come down a little from that stratospheric level of the opening few games. But Alcaraz then lets off a rocket of a forehand that clips the sideline and that’s the game.
 Share 2h ago 08.30 EST First set: Alcaraz* 3-2 Cobolli (*denotes next server) 
 Cobolli’s vibe is similar to Alcaraz’s – with his quick feet, superb shotmaking and showmanship – but he doesn’t quite have Alcaraz’s level of concentration and consistency. That’s the challenge for the 24-year-old Italian next year, if he wants to win the game’s biggest prizes. The French Open runner-up keeps his eye in in this game, though, nailing an unreturned serve down the T on game point to seal it to 15.
 View image in fullscreen Flavio Cobolli has trouble matching Carlos Alcaraz early on. Photograph: Guglielmo Mangiapane/Reuters Share Updated at  08.34 EST 2h ago 08.27 EST First set: Alcaraz 3-1 Cobolli* (*denotes next server) 
 Cobolli finds a few first serves to secure his first hold, to 30, and get his name on the scoreboard, having been bagelled in the second set of his 7-6, 6-0 defeat by Tiafoe on Wednesday. But Alcaraz, showing a perfect balance of aggression and control, claims another commanding hold to maintain his advantage. Already it’s showtime for Alcaraz and already it’s looking ominous for Cobolli.
 Share 2h ago 08.21 EST First set: Alcaraz 2-0 Cobolli* (*denotes next server) 
 15-0, 30-0, 40-0. Cobolli then raises the biggest cheer so far from his home crowd with a forehand return winner, and he’s holding his arms in the air as if he’s broken back, but it’s still only 40-15 and Alcaraz wraps up the game on the next point by stepping forward to the net and finishing things with a beautiful backhand volley. What injury?! Alcaraz has started exactly where he left off against Medvedev and Tiafoe and his outstanding late-season form looks set to continue.
 Share Updated at  10.32 EST 2h ago 08.18 EST Alcaraz breaks: Alcaraz* 1-0 Cobolli (*denotes next server) 
 Ready? Let’s play. Cobolli won eight straight points at start of his match against Tiafoe, before fading fast, and it’s a quick start here, as he rips a cross-court forehand winner for 15-0. But very soon it all falls apart, and Alcaraz has break points at 15-40. Alcaraz doesn’t take the first but he does the second, and that was a cheap concession from Cobolli. Alcaraz’s hamstring hasn’t even really been tested yet.
 Share 2h ago 08.13 EST Alcaraz is looking like a 43-year-old rather than a 23-year-old out there, with strapping on his left hamstring, tape on his right knee and an arm sleeve to protect his right wrist. These two have surprisingly met only once before, by the way, back in 2023 at the French Open, with Alcaraz winning in straight sets in the first round.
 Share 2h ago 08.09 EST Jamie Murray muses on Sky that Alcaraz most likely didn’t get out of bed this morning doing back flips, given his physical predicament . Alcaraz does win the coin flip though, and he elects to receive. He wants to test Cobolli’s nerves on serve.
 Share 2h ago 08.06 EST “Buongiorno!” emails Simon Wylie. “ Several people (from my own family) have commented on the level of pedantry to which I dragged everyone down yesterday with my Italian plural comment.” I could do with Simon translating right now, though, because there’s plenty being said over the stadium’s speakers but non capisco . There’s a nice embrace between Alcaraz and Cobolli before they walk on to court – these two are good friends who have trained together before – and it’s the home player, with a cheeky wink, who arrives first, before Alcaraz, held together by all his strapping, follows.
 Share 3h ago 07.58 EST In other news today: 
 Men’s tennis boosts prize money for players to more than $350m in major overhaul Read more Share 3h ago 07.57 EST Tumaini Carayol Leon Smith will step down from his role as Great Britain’s Davis Cup captain at the end of this month after 16 years in the position. Britain’s appearance in the Davis Cup Finals next week will mark his final competition.
 Smith has enjoyed one of the longest tenures as a Davis Cup captain in the sport’s history and the longest by a British Davis Cup captain. The highlight of his term was Britain’s historic Davis Cup triumph in 2015, a team also led by his childhood friend Andy Murray.
 Smith said: “It has been an enormous privilege to lead the team for so many years, and I feel now is the right time, both for me personally and for the team moving forwards.”
 Smith had been considering his resignation for some months and the LTA has already started planning for his successor, with the new Davis Cup captain expected to be announced in the coming weeks. Smith will continue his role as the LTA’s head of men’s tennis, which he took on at the same time that he became Davis Cup captain in 2010.
 Share 3h ago 07.55 EST Skupski’s also got next week’s Davis Cup Finals to look forward to, which will be Leon Smith’s final event as Britain’s captain , after the LTA announced today that he’s stepping down after 16 years in the role. Smith will be remembered, of course, for guiding the team to their first Davis Cup title in 79 years in 2015 – it’s not believed that Andy Murray, who spearheaded that win, is interested in taking over the role at this time.
 Share Updated at  07.56 EST 3h ago 07.52 EST Already today in the doubles, Britain’s Neal Skupski and his American partner Christian Harrison , the reigning Australian and US Open champions in a fine first season together, have snatched the last semi-final spot with a 7-6 (5), 6-4 win over Spain’s Marcel Granollers and Argentina’s Horacio Zeballos.
 Share 3h ago 07.34 EST Alcaraz is practising on an outside court at the moment. He’s got heavy strapping around that left hamstring, as well as tape on his right knee, and he’s barely got out of first gear yet, as he cautiously warms up. He’s hitting a lot closer to a match than he normally would, probably because he doesn’t want to risk the hamstring seizing up between practice and facing Cobolli.
 View image in fullscreen The scene right now. Photograph: Guglielmo Mangiapane/Reuters Share 3h ago 07.26 EST Share 3h ago 07.24 EST Share 3h ago 07.23 EST In the John McEnroe group yesterday, Alexander Zverev finished top with his third straight-sets win out of three , though Arthur Fils ( and his nuclear forehand ) made the world No 1 work for the 6-4, 7-6 victory, while Ben Shelton qualified for the semi-finals for the first time after seeing off the winless Rafael Jodar 7-6, 7-5.
 Zverev will now face the victor of tonight’s straight shoot-out between Daniil Medvedev and Frances Tiafoe, and Shelton will meet Alcaraz in a rematch of that US Open quarter-final. Yes please (though hopefully this one won’t finish at 3.30am …)
 Share 3h ago 07.04 EST And talking about Agassi: this is a lovely trip down memory lane of the 1990 season-ending final. 
 Share Updated at  07.06 EST 4h ago 07.01 EST Preamble
 Buongiorno ! With Carlos Alcaraz already guaranteed to finish top of the Ivan Lendl group after two straight-sets wins, the biggest jeopardy going into his match against the already-eliminated Flavio Cobolli is the state of his left hamstring. After picking up the injury against Daniil Medvedev on Wednesday , Alcaraz had an MRI scan yesterday and was cleared to play on, so now we’ll get to see if he can still hit the absurd levels he did earlier this week.
 While Alcaraz is riding a late-season wave after his wrist injury-enforced summer hiatus, sweeping up titles in Tokyo, Vienna and Paris, Cobolli was reduced to tears after the 7-6, 6-0 loss to Frances Tiafoe that sealed his exit two days ago. The Italian – the only home player in the Jannik Sinner-less singles – said it was the saddest match of his career and that he felt he’d let the Turin crowd down on his ATP Finals debut. But Cobolli still described today’s meeting with Alcaraz – just the second of his career – as “a beautiful gift … I hope to annoy him as much as possible, even if it won’t be easy”.
 A description of Cobolli’s style – rapid feet, flashy shotmaking, great hands and effortless charisma – could of course be used for Alcaraz too, and it was actually training with Alcaraz a few years ago in Spain that flicked a switch in Cobolli and transformed his work ethic. This match represents a free shot for the French Open runner-up against a player he admires so much and gets on with so well, while for Alcaraz it’s a chance to test his hamstring with no pressure on the result.
 Alcaraz won’t take any unnecessary risks with the injury – he’s got the Davis Cup Finals to come next week too and he probably still has those missed four months at the back of his mind – but if he’s fit, yet another piece of tennis history is his for the taking. Having started his ATP season by becoming the youngest man to complete a career grand slam, he could end it by joining Agassi, Federer and Djokovic as only the fourth man in history to have won all four majors and the season finale. It’s so good to have him back; let’s hope this latest injury doesn’t force him away again.
 Play begins at: about 1pm GMT/2pm local time. Andiamo !
